title: What They Never Taught You: Real Talk about Your Creative Career
note: Placeholder transcript for the AI Week demo, not a real transcription. Replace via generate_transcripts.py once ffmpeg + an OpenAI/Whisper key are available.

segments.text: Yuko Shimizu opens by describing the jump from art school to freelance illustration, and why nobody teaches you how to actually run a creative career as a business.
She walks through building an early portfolio: picking a consistent visual voice over chasing trends, and why a scattered portfolio confuses art directors more than a narrow one.
A section on rejection: pitching book covers and editorial work that never got picked, and reframing a 'no' as information about fit rather than a verdict on the work itself.
Deep dive into her materials and technique - ink, brush pens, and how a hybrid analog-then-digital workflow keeps linework expressive instead of overly polished.
Working with publishers and art directors: negotiating scope, revisions, and usage rights on editorial and book-cover commissions without underselling the work.
Talks candidly about imposter syndrome persisting even after awards and major clients, and the daily habits she uses to keep working through it.
On teaching: what she tells illustration students at SVA that she wishes someone had told her - namely that technical skill matters less than a distinct point of view.
Turning personal, non-commissioned projects into new client relationships, and using social platforms to build an audience independent of any single publisher.
Closing thoughts on AI image tools: her take on where generative tools help an illustrator's process versus where a distinct hand-drawn voice is what clients are actually paying for.
